How is Georgia set up for selling a house?

Georgia is split into 159 counties, and almost every step of a home sale runs through one of them. That is the first thing to sort out, because the county decides who values your house, who collects the tax bill and where the deed gets recorded.

Fulton County, home to Atlanta, is the most populous. Peach County, created in 1924, is the newest. A small rural county and metro Atlanta follow the same state law, yet the offices you deal with can run very differently.

Four county offices come up in nearly every sale:

  • The board of tax assessors, which sets the value of the property.
  • The tax commissioner, who collects the bill and takes homestead applications.
  • The clerk of superior court, where deeds and liens are recorded.
  • The probate court, which handles estates, including a house left by someone who died.

The county list below links to our local guides. If your county has none, call these offices directly before you sign anything.

Who collects property tax when I sell in Georgia?

The county tax commissioner collects it, and the county board of tax assessors sets the value. Georgia's Department of Revenue explains that assessed value is 40 percent of fair market value, and that property is valued as of January 1 each year.

The January 1 date matters at closing. Whoever owned the house on that day owes the full year's bill, and the Department says Georgia law does not allow a refund to someone who owned for only part of the year. Our Georgia property tax guide walks through the appeal and payment steps in more detail.

ItemWhat the Department of Revenue says
Assessed value40 percent of fair market value
Valuation dateJanuary 1 of each year
Usual due dateDecember 20 in most counties, with some counties using other dates
Time to pay after billing60 days from the billing date
Appeal window45 days from the date the assessment notice was mailed
Standard state homestead exemption$2,000 off the assessed value, for county and school taxes

An appeal starts in writing with the board of tax assessors. The owner then picks one of three routes: the board of equalization, a hearing officer or an arbitrator.

The homestead exemption applies to the home you live in as your legal residence. You apply with the county tax commissioner, and in some counties with the assessor. Unpaid taxes can end in a tax sale, which we explain on our Georgia tax sale page.

How does foreclosure work in Georgia?

Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state, so a lender can foreclose without filing a lawsuit or going before a judge. The Attorney General's office points to O.C.G.A. 44-14-162 through 44-14-162.4 as the governing statutes.

The sequence the Attorney General describes runs like this:

  • The lender sends a written notice of intent to foreclose at least 30 days before the proposed sale, by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.
  • That notice names someone with authority to negotiate or modify the loan and includes a copy of the sale advertisement.
  • The sale is advertised in the county's legal newspaper for four consecutive weeks.
  • The sale takes place on the courthouse steps on the first Tuesday of the month, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.

After the sale, the new owner can file a dispossessory action to remove the borrower. If the sale price falls short of the debt, the lender may pursue a deficiency in court.

The Attorney General lists curing the default, a short sale, a deed in lieu and bankruptcy as ways out, and a bankruptcy filed before the sale stays the proceeding. Our Georgia foreclosure guide covers it step by step, and HUD-certified counseling is available at 1-800-569-4287.

What does Georgia transfer tax cost a seller?

The state real estate transfer tax is $1 for the first $1,000 of the sale price, plus 10 cents for each additional $100. That works out to about $1 per $1,000 of price.

The Department of Revenue says the seller is liable, though many sales contracts say the buyer will pay it. It must be paid before the deed can be recorded with the clerk of superior court, and the clerk then attaches a certification that it was paid. Questions about exemptions go to the county clerk.

Sale priceTransfer tax at the posted rate
$150,000$150
$300,000$300
$450,000$450

The dollar figures are our arithmetic from the published rate, so confirm the exact amount with your closing attorney. Other costs depend on the contract and the lender, which our Georgia closing costs page lays out. If you are thinking about moving title by a quitclaim deed, read our quitclaim deed guide first, since that deed carries no warranty of ownership.

Do I need an attorney to close a Georgia home sale?

In practice, yes. The Georgia Supreme Court approved Unauthorized Practice of Law Advisory Opinion 2003-2, which says only a licensed Georgia attorney may prepare or facilitate the signing of a deed of conveyance. The Court also said a lawyer cannot hand off a closing to a non-lawyer, and it rejected witness-only closings.

That is why Georgia sales are often called attorney closings. The attorney handling the file typically examines title, prepares the deed, collects funds and records the paperwork. Ask who the attorney represents and what the fee is before you agree to a closing date.

What happens if I inherited a house in Georgia?

Probate runs through the probate court of the county where the person lived at death. A personal representative, called an executor when there is a will or an administrator when there is not, is usually the person who can sign a sale. Our Georgia probate guide has the longer version.

Two facts help families plan. First, Georgia levies no state estate tax or inheritance tax, according to the Department of Revenue, which cites O.C.G.A. 48-12-1. Second, a surviving spouse or minor children can petition for a year's support, which sets part of the estate aside for them. The petition is due within 24 months of the death, and it can be filed even if there is a will. More background is on our Georgia estate tax page.

Can I sell a Georgia house that has tenants?

You can list or sell a rented house, but the tenants have rights that continue after the sale. Georgia courts explain that a landlord cannot evict without filing a dispossessory action and getting a court order, and removing a tenant without that process is against the law.

  • A tenant has 7 days from actual service of a dispossessory warrant to answer. If day 7 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next day.
  • If a rented property is foreclosed, the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act lets tenants stay at least 90 days or through the lease, whichever is longer. A new owner who plans to live there may only be held to 90 days.

The courts page does not set out a pre-filing notice rule, so check the local magistrate court before you act. We cover the process on our Georgia eviction page and the broader rules on our landlord and tenant page.

What property problems come up when selling in Georgia?

Radon and septic systems are the two the state itself talks about most. The Environmental Protection Agency's Georgia map sorts counties into three radon zones, and Zone 1 means a predicted indoor average above 4 pCi/L. The agency says all homes should be tested regardless of zone. The Georgia Department of Public Health says northern Georgia, with metro Atlanta named in particular, has higher radon levels because of the geology, and that a home should be fixed at 4 pCi/L or above.

For septic, the Department of Public Health's homeowner guide says county health departments permit and inspect these systems, and that repairs need a repair permit. The county health department can supply the inspection record showing the system's type and location. Many lenders ask for a system evaluation at closing, so keep your pumping receipts.

What does a cash, as-is sale mean in Georgia?

It means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and the sale does not depend on a loan approval. Georgia law does not change for it. The same transfer tax, recording and attorney closing steps apply, and any mortgage or lien is paid from the proceeds.

What changes is the work on your side. You skip listing prep, showings and most repair negotiations. Weigh that against what a listed sale could bring after prep time and cost. With a lien or foreclosure date, the calendar may matter more.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Georgia have?

Georgia has 159 counties. Records, tax bills and probate cases run through the county.

When are Georgia property taxes due?

The Department of Revenue says taxes are normally due December 20 in most counties, with 60 days to pay from the billing date. Some counties differ, so check your bill.

Who pays the Georgia transfer tax?

The seller is liable under the Department of Revenue's rules, although contracts often assign it to the buyer. Check your contract.

Is foreclosure in Georgia handled by a court?

No. Georgia uses non-judicial foreclosure. The lender must give written notice at least 30 days before a sale held on the first Tuesday of the month.

Does Georgia have an inheritance tax?

The Department of Revenue says Georgia has no inheritance tax and no state estate tax for decedents dying after 2004.

Do I have to use an attorney to close?

Georgia's Supreme Court has said only a licensed Georgia attorney may prepare deeds and oversee closings, so plan on attorney involvement.

Can a tenant be removed before I sell?

Only through a court. The landlord files a dispossessory action, and the tenant has 7 days from service to answer.

Should I test for radon before listing?

The Environmental Protection Agency says all homes should be tested. Georgia's health department suggests fixing a home at 4 pCi/L or above.
